title: "quarto-index id-collision probe"
toc: true
from: markdown-smart
filters:
  - index
---

# Names the document has already taken

Generated ids step over any name the document itself uses, however that name
was written. This document claims five, in the five spellings the extension
reads: a Pandoc attribute, and raw HTML with a double-quoted, an unquoted and
an uppercase-`ID=` attribute, plus a raw *inline* one — the extension reads raw
inlines as well as raw blocks, and single quotes as well as double.

One term is marked here: [zeta]{.index}. Another, twice: [eta]{.index}, and
[eta]{.index}.

::: {#qi-index}
A div claiming the generated section's own id, written as a Pandoc attribute.
Deliberately not a heading: Quarto moves a heading's id onto the section
wrapper it builds, which would put the claim somewhere the author did not
write it.
:::

```{=html}
<p id="qi-index-1">Raw HTML, double-quoted.</p>
<p id=qi-index-2>Raw HTML, unquoted.</p>
<p ID="qi-index-3">Raw HTML, uppercase attribute name.</p>
```

A raw inline claims the fifth: `<span id='qi-index-4'>single-quoted</span>`{=html}.

::: {.qi-index-here}
:::

# Names a mark and another element both claim

An id the author wrote on a mark is the mark's link target, and an id written
anywhere else on the page belongs to whatever the author wrote it on. Where the
two are the same name, the mark is the one that yields: the extension writes
only its own spans, so it anchors the mark on a minted id, reports the refusal,
and the other element keeps the name it was given. One mark per spelling the id
census reads, so a claim written in raw HTML weighs exactly as a Pandoc
attribute does.

A Pandoc attribute claims one: [alpha]{#shared-attr .index}.

::: {#shared-attr}
A div claiming the name the alpha mark was written with.
:::

Raw HTML claims three more: [beta]{#shared-dq .index}, [gamma]{#shared-uq
.index} and [delta]{#shared-up .index}.

```{=html}
<p id="shared-dq">Raw HTML, double-quoted.</p>
<p id=shared-uq>Raw HTML, unquoted.</p>
<p ID="shared-up">Raw HTML, uppercase attribute name.</p>
```

A raw inline claims the fifth: [epsilon]{#shared-sq .index} against
`<span id='shared-sq'>single-quoted</span>`{=html}.

A sixth is a name the numbering would otherwise mint, so a claim on one of
those is refused exactly as any other claim is rather than being handed over by
the mint: [theta]{#qi-mark-3 .index}.

```{=html}
<p id="qi-mark-3">Raw HTML claiming a name the numbering mints.</p>
```

# Two marks written with one name

Neither mark is anything but a mark, so document order settles which keeps the
name: [kappa]{#twin .index} comes first and keeps it, and [lambda]{#twin
.index} yields.

# Names nothing contests

A mark whose id no other element carries keeps it, whatever the name is. Three
here: one nobody else wrote, [mu]{#solo .index}; one in the heading below,
which is where an anchor cannot sit, so the id moves to an empty span just
after it; and one spelled as a name the numbering would otherwise mint,
[xi]{#qi-mark-9 .index}, which the numbering steps over as it always has.

## A heading carrying [nu]{#in-heading .index}

Text under that heading, so the section is not empty.

# Names only a comment carries

An HTML comment is not part of the rendered page: an id written inside one is
on nothing a link can reach, so it contests nothing and a mark keeps the name
it was written with. Two here, one per shape a comment arrives in — a comment
written on its own, and one inside a raw HTML block: [omicron]{#in-comment
.index}, and [pi]{#in-raw-comment .index}.

<!-- An earlier draft of this paragraph: <p id="in-comment">gone</p>. -->

```{=html}
<p id="kept-alive">Raw HTML beside a comment.</p>
<!-- <p id="in-raw-comment">also gone</p> -->
```

The links an author writes to those marks still resolve: [to omicron](#in-comment)
and [to pi](#in-raw-comment).

# Cross-references and a name something else claims

A mark that only points at another entry files no locator, so nothing the index
writes links to it. It carries an id all the same, and one id still names one
element: where something else on the page claims that name, the mark yields it
and says so. No locator moves, there having been none.

A `see=` mark against a div claiming its name: [rho]{#xref-dup .index see="mu"}.

::: {#xref-dup}
A div claiming the name the rho mark was written with.
:::

A `see-also=` mark against raw HTML claiming its name: [sigma]{#xref-raw .index
see-also="mu"}.

```{=html}
<p id="xref-raw">Raw HTML claiming the name the sigma mark was written with.</p>
```

A cross-reference mark whose name nothing else claims keeps it, and nothing is
reported: [upsilon]{#xref-solo .index see="mu"}.

## A heading carrying [tau]{#xref-heading .index see="mu"}

A cross-reference mark written in a heading, whose id Quarto would otherwise
copy into the table of contents. The name is claimed below as well, so this
mark yields it where the relocated anchor lands.

::: {#xref-heading}
A div claiming the name the tau mark was written with.
:::

# A cross-reference and a locator mark written with one name

Where two marks share a name and one of them files a locator, the locator mark
keeps it whichever is written first: a reader follows the locator, and nothing
the index writes points at a cross-reference. The cross-reference comes first
here and yields anyway: [phi]{#twin-xref .index see="mu"}, then
[chi]{#twin-xref .index}.

# A mark this filter leaves alone, inside a heading

A mark whose content yields no text and that carries no `entry=` indexes
nothing, so the filter returns it untouched: the `.index` class and the id its
author wrote are both still on the span. It gives up no name and files no
locator. Its id has to leave the heading all the same — the table of contents
copies a heading's inlines, so an id left inside one is on two elements of the
page. That is why this document sets `toc: true`.

## A heading carrying [![](dot.png)]{#untagged-in-heading .index}

Text under that heading, so the section is not empty.

# Names a reader that does not read markup would miss

The census reads raw HTML the way a browser does: an `id=` counts where it is
an attribute of an opening tag, and nowhere else. Two names turn on that. One
is claimed by a real element standing after a neighbour whose attribute VALUE
contains what looks like the opening of a comment, so a reader that cut the
text at the first `<!--` would never reach the claim and would leave the mark
carrying a contested name in silence: [psi]{#hidden-carrier .index}. The other
is written in the text of a `script` element, which is character data rather
than markup and renders no element at all, so it contests nothing and the mark
keeps it: [omega]{#in-script .index}. The two are written in raw blocks of
their own, so neither name's fate depends on the other's block being read.

```{=html}
<script>var draft = "<p id='in-script'>";</script>
```

```{=html}
<p title="looks like <!-- a comment">Raw HTML whose attribute value opens what is not a comment.</p>
<p id="hidden-carrier">Raw HTML claiming the name the psi mark was written with.</p>
```

The link an author writes to the second still resolves: [to omega](#in-script).

# Names an element standing after a skipped one carries

A browser reads the text content of seven elements as text rather than as
markup — `script`, `style`, `xmp`, `iframe`, `noembed`, `noframes` and
`textarea` — steps over it, and goes on reading the markup that follows. So
does the census. A name written on a real element standing AFTER one of those
seven, in that same raw HTML block, is on an element of the rendered page like
any other, so a mark written with it yields it.

Six here, one per element bar the last: [after-script]{#beyond-script .index},
[after-style]{#beyond-style .index}, [after-xmp]{#beyond-xmp .index},
[after-iframe]{#beyond-iframe .index}, [after-noembed]{#beyond-noembed .index}
and [after-noframes]{#beyond-noframes .index}. Each element and the claim after
it are written in one block, which is what a walk that abandons the rest of a
block after the first of them fails to read.

```{=html}
<script>var draft = "not markup";</script>
<p id="beyond-script">Raw HTML after a script element, in that same block.</p>
```

```{=html}
<style>.qi-not-markup { color: red }</style>
<p id=beyond-style>Raw HTML after a style element, in that same block.</p>
```

```{=html}
<xmp>not markup</xmp>
<p ID="beyond-xmp">Raw HTML after an xmp element, in that same block.</p>
```

```{=html}
<iframe>not markup</iframe>
<p id='beyond-iframe'>Raw HTML after an iframe element, in that same block.</p>
```

```{=html}
<noembed>not markup</noembed>
<p id="beyond-noembed">Raw HTML after a noembed element, in that same block.</p>
```

```{=html}
<noframes>not markup</noframes>
<p id=beyond-noframes>Raw HTML after a noframes element, in that same block.</p>
```

## A heading carrying [after-textarea]{#beyond-textarea .index}

The seventh, written in a heading: the name is claimed below it, so the mark
yields, and the minted id it is given lands on the empty span after the heading
rather than on the mark's own.

```{=html}
<textarea>not markup</textarea>
<p id="beyond-textarea">Raw HTML after a textarea element, in that same block.</p>
```

# Names written in a skipped element's own text

Inside those same seven elements an `id=` is text and not an attribute: the
page renders no element carrying it, so it contests nothing and a mark written
with it keeps it. Seven here, one per element, two of them claimed by a raw
INLINE rather than by a raw block, the census reading both:
[inside-script]{#buried-script .index}, [inside-style]{#buried-style .index},
[inside-xmp]{#buried-xmp .index}, [inside-iframe]{#buried-iframe .index},
[inside-noembed]{#buried-noembed .index}, [inside-noframes]{#buried-noframes
.index} and [inside-textarea]{#buried-textarea .index}.

```{=html}
<script>var draft = "<p id='buried-script'>gone</p>";</script>
<style>/* <p id=buried-style>gone</p> */</style>
<xmp><p ID="buried-xmp">gone</p></xmp>
<iframe><p id="buried-iframe">gone</p></iframe>
<noembed><p id="buried-noembed">gone</p></noembed>
```

Two claimed by raw inlines: `<noframes><p id='buried-noframes'>gone</p></noframes>`{=html}
and `<textarea><p id="buried-textarea">gone</p></textarea>`{=html}.

The links an author writes to two of those marks still resolve:
[to inside-script](#buried-script) and [to inside-textarea](#buried-textarea).

# An end tag one of those elements only looks like

Such an element ends at its own end tag and at nothing else. `</scriptx>` is
not the end of a `script`: the text runs on past it, and a name written after
it is still inside the element. A real end tag may carry whitespace before its
`>` all the same, and the text ends there.

Written past a lookalike, so the name is still in the element's text and its
mark keeps it: [false-end-script]{#veiled-script .index} and
[false-end-textarea]{#veiled-textarea .index}.

Written past a real end tag spelled with a space, so the name is on an element
of the page and its mark yields it: [spaced-end-script]{#past-spaced-script
.index} and [spaced-end-textarea]{#past-spaced-textarea .index}.

```{=html}
<script>var draft = '</scriptx> <p id="veiled-script">gone</p>';</script>
<script>var kept = 1;</script > <p ID="past-spaced-script">Raw HTML after a real end tag spelled with a space.</p>
<textarea>not markup</textarea > <p id=past-spaced-textarea>Raw HTML after a real end tag spelled with a space.</p>
```

The fourth is claimed by a raw inline: `<textarea>x</textareax> <p id='veiled-textarea'>gone</p></textarea>`{=html}.

# Names written on a closing tag

An attribute on a closing tag is on nothing: the tag's name is read and the
rest dropped, so the element it closes never carries the name and no element of
the rendered page does. Two here, one per spelling:
[on-closing-p]{#closing-p .index} and [on-closing-em]{#closing-em .index}.

The block below closes a `p` and an `em`, neither of which is open where it
stands, so neither tag closes anything at all.

```{=html}
</p id="closing-p">
</em id=closing-em>
```
